title: Polling Shared Flags Without a Valid Synchronization Protocol
pattern: A loop waits for another thread's state transition, readiness, shutdown, or termination by repeatedly reading a plain shared flag without the language/platform protocol needed for valid concurrent access and visibility.
why_bad: Invalid shared accesses can have undefined behavior in the language model, permit cached/hoisted loads (the compiler may load the flag into a register once and never re-read it), or fail to establish visibility of data published with the flag. The loop may never terminate or may continue with stale associated data.
detection: Trace the loop's flag reads and the concurrent writes, then assess them under the actual memory model. (1) Rust and standard C/C++: concurrent conflicting plain accesses without synchronization constitute a data race; a compiler fence or `volatile` qualifier alone does not repair them. (2) Kernel/platform code: inspect the documented marked-access and memory-ordering protocol (e.g. `READ_ONCE()` paired with `WRITE_ONCE()`/barriers), not merely whether `READ_ONCE` appears. In both cases confirm that the loop really observes another thread rather than ordinary single-threaded state.
counterexample: Single-threaded variables are outside scope. Correct atomic or blocking synchronization with a suitable publication protocol is legitimate, e.g. spinning on `std::sync::atomic::AtomicBool` with explicit memory ordering. Platform marked loads such as `READ_ONCE()` are acceptable only under that platform's documented concurrent-access rules and only for the guarantees the protocol actually needs; `volatile` alone is not a portable thread-synchronization exemption.
source: Paul E. McKenney, *Is Parallel Programming Hard?*, Listing 4.19.; Paul E. McKenney, *Is Parallel Programming Hard...*, Listing 4.19 / passage [4, 5, 299].; Paul McKenney Appendix C.3, Appendix E.15
